item.title: Inkling-2-Mini in 5.4 GB Memory (310 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://github.com/ShinMegamiBoson/lookatmyquant, See on Hacker News

LookAtMyQuant is a quantization compiler. It measures how much each stored piece of a model hurts the output when compressed. It then picks a code for each piece so the whole model fits a size budget with the least damage.

On Gemma 4 E2B, its GGUF has 12× lower KL than Q4_K_M at the same file size. The method and every result are on the site.

The code is under the MIT license.

LookAtMyQuant 2: Qwen3.5-4B in 1.2 GB

LookAtMyQuant 2 takes Qwen3.5-4B to 1.23 GB, 2.3 bits per weight. The file solves 330 of 540 exact-answer math problems. Prism ML's Bonsai 2 Ternary 4B solves 328 at 1.20 GB, and the original solves 359. Its KL from the original on held-out text is 0.45 nats, against 0.59 for Bonsai.

The recipe is post-training quantization with trellis codes, calibrated on the model's own worked math solutions with digit tokens weighted 10×, and with bits allocated per row by Fisher information. 4,000 steps of distillation follow, in which every layer is re-quantized once from the original weights. The page has the findings, the full recipe and its cost, about $34 of GPU time.

The recipe's code is here, and the next section runs it. The 1.23 GB file itself is the lm2-qwen35-4b-1.2gb release, packed for the Apple Silicon runtime.

Qwen3.8-27B in 7.2 GB

The same recipe takes Qwen3.8-27B from 53.7 GB to 7.2 GB, 2.1 bits per weight, calibrated and distilled on English prose and chat, code and math. The file solves 401 of the 540 math problems, as many as the original, and Unsloth's UD-IQ2_XXS GGUF of the same size solves 348. It also scores above that GGUF on HumanEval (73.8% against 67.1%), MMLU (78.8% against 75.0%) and GSM8K (94.5% against 92.7%).

Beside it sits a 4-bit DSpine drafter (1.02 GB, converted from tencent/Qwen3.8-27B-DSpine-b16 with runtime_mlx/convert_dspine.py and packed with pack_drafter.py), which roughly doubles decode speed on math and code on Apple silicon.

Inkling-2-Mini in 5.4 GB and 8.9 GB

The same compiler and proximal fine-tuning (SQYFR), extended to a 26.4B physical / 5.4B active 3×-looped MoE (L6–17 looped 3× = 48 logical visits, 128 experts top-8), compresses thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini from 18.89 GB of text weights to 5.38 GB (1.63 bits/weight) and 8.87 GB (2.69 bits/weight) using 4 KB SRAM hashed block-vector trellis codes (ht2/ht3), row trellis codes (rtr1/rtr4), and a tr2 floor on the tail lm_head bucket (head.7).

Evaluated on the same BF16 teacher, openai/gsm8k (test[:200], greedy, reasoning_effort="none"), all 164 executable openai/openai_humaneval problems, 4 Vision VQA tests (with the untouched 637 MB BF16 vision tower), and 16+13-language TextMix windows:

Model Text GB free_KL (en/chat/code) all13_KL GSM8K (200) HumanEval (164) Pooled vs Teacher
Original BF16 Teacher 18.89 0.0000 0.0000 147 / 200 (73.5%) 66 / 164 (40.2%) 100.0%
LookAtMyQuant 5.4 GB (SQYFR) 5.38 0.0895 0.2871 134 / 200 (67.0%) 60 / 164 (36.6%) 91.2%
Unsloth UD-IQ1_S 7.76 0.0808 0.1236 127 / 200 (63.5%) 46 / 164 (28.0%) 81.6%
LookAtMyQuant 8.9 GB (SQYFR) 8.87 0.0208 0.0571 148 / 200 (74.0%) 58 / 164 (35.4%) 96.8%
Unsloth UD-Q2_K_XL 9.14 0.0486 0.0811 132 / 200 (66.0%) 49 / 164 (29.9%) 85.3%
Unsloth UD-IQ3_XXS 11.66 0.0189 0.0278 148 / 200 (74.0%) 68 / 164 (41.5%) 101.4%

At 5.38 GB, Inkling-2-Mini-LookAtMyQuant-5.4GB outscores Unsloth's 9.14 GB UD-Q2_K_XL on both GSM8K and HumanEval at 41% smaller size (up from 76/200 and 24/164 untuned). At 8.87 GB, Inkling-2-Mini-LookAtMyQuant-8.9GB matches the BF16 original on GSM8K and cuts KL 2.34× on English/chat/code and 29.6% across all 13 languages below UD-Q2_K_XL. Both run directly through lamq and runtime_mlx with custom Apple Silicon Metal kernels (including M5 MetalPerformancePrimitives MoE prefill + FlashAttention-2 SDPA + exact unbiased temp > 0 speculative sampling, plus opt-in dynamic sigmoid Top-K routing, tight-margin verify, and N-gram prompt lookup), optionally paired with the 178.9 MB 4-bit DSpark drafters: on M5 Max, 5.4 GB reaches 1,807 tok/s T=512 prefill (1,047 tok/s at T=128), 75.3 tok/s serial decode, and 124.4 tok/s median lossless drafted decode (142.9 tok/s math, 126.5 tok/s reasoning, 122.2 tok/s code, 104.0 tok/s prose; up to ~150–160 tok/s with opt-in top6 / max_logit_gap=0.30; 5.98 GB active RAM), and 8.9 GB decodes at 63.5 tok/s serial and 106.0 tok/s median (125.8 tok/s reasoning, 123.8 tok/s math; 9.41 GB active RAM).

Install and use the Apple Silicon runtime

On Apple silicon, install the runtime package directly (this installs mlx, mlx-lm, numpy, and huggingface-hub without the PyTorch compiler dependencies):

pip install git+https://github.com/ShinMegamiBoson/lookatmyquant.git

From a local clone, pip install -e . installs the lamq command, or run python -m runtime_mlx without installing.

Command line. Pass either a local model folder or a Hugging Face repo ID:

lamq generate shinmegamiboson/Qwen3.8-27B-LookAtMyQuant-7.2GB \
    -p "What is 17 times 23? Show the steps."

lamq generate shinmegamiboson/Qwen3.8-27B-LookAtMyQuant-7.2GB \
    --drafter shinmegamiboson/Qwen3.8-27B-LookAtMyQuant-7.2GB-drafter \
    -p "Write a Python function that merges overlapping intervals." --stats

lamq chat shinmegamiboson/Qwen3.8-27B-LookAtMyQuant-7.2GB \
    --drafter shinmegamiboson/Qwen3.8-27B-LookAtMyQuant-7.2GB-drafter

lamq generate shinmegamiboson/Inkling-2-Mini-LookAtMyQuant-5.4GB \
    --drafter shinmegamiboson/Inkling-2-Mini-LookAtMyQuant-drafter \
    -p "What is 17 times 23? Show the steps." --stats

lamq generate reads stdin when -p is omitted, supports --raw, --system, --thinking, --temp, --mode linear|chat-fork|copy-wide, --no-adaptive, and --json. lamq info <model> inspects a packed model's format and dimensions without loading weights.

Python integration. runtime_mlx.load returns an (model, tokenizer) pair compatible with mlx_lm.generate and mlx_lm.stream_generate (auto-detecting opgraph-packed-1 models such as Qwen3.5-4B / Qwen3.8-27B and lamq.json exports such as Gemma 4 E2B):

from mlx_lm import generate
from runtime_mlx import load

model, tok = load("shinmegamiboson/Qwen3.8-27B-LookAtMyQuant-7.2GB")
prompt = tok.apply_chat_template(
    [{"role": "user", "content": "What is 17 times 23? Show the steps."}],
    add_generation_prompt=True,
    enable_thinking=False,
)
print(generate(model, tok, prompt, max_tokens=200))

For streaming, multi-turn chat, or speculative decoding through one interface, use Runtime:

from runtime_mlx import Runtime

rt = Runtime.load(
    "shinmegamiboson/Qwen3.8-27B-LookAtMyQuant-7.2GB",
    drafter="shinmegamiboson/Qwen3.8-27B-LookAtMyQuant-7.2GB-drafter",
)
for chunk in rt.stream("Solve 3x + 4y = 31 and 5x - 2y = 17.", max_tokens=256):
    print(chunk.text, end="", flush=True)

Run the compiler on SmolLM2-360M in three commands

Install the dependencies and download the model and WikiText-2. The code reads SmolLM2-360M's config when it starts, so do this first.

pip install -r requirements.txt
python -c "from huggingface_hub import snapshot_download as d; d('HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-360M')"
python -c "from datasets import load_dataset as l; l('Salesforce/wikitext', 'wikitext-2-raw-v1')"

Measure. This compresses one piece at a time, leaves the rest exact, and records the KL to the original model. The full set for this model, 2,312 measurements, took about 50 minutes on an L40S.

python compiler.py measure --model HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-360M --part linear --layers 0-3 --out results/batch/my_measurements.json

Allocate. This picks one code per piece, with the least summed KL inside the budget. It needs no GPU. This command uses the SmolLM2-360M measurements in this repository, with a budget of 3.044 bits per weight.

python compiler.py allocate --sens 'results/batch/ccSens*.json' --target disk --items linear --bits 3.044 --out results/compiler/plans/my_plan.json

The plan it writes has the same widths as results/compiler/plans/sm_lin_3044.json.

Build and score. This quantizes the model to the plan, one matrix at a time. It then reports perplexity and KL to the original on WikiText-2 test.

python quantize.py --program plan --model HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-360M --plan results/compiler/plans/my_plan.json --out results/my_run.json

Our run of that plan is in results/batch/cc_sm_lin_3044.json. It reached perplexity 16.64 and KL 0.0926, against an original perplexity of 15.31. Add --layers 1 --calib 8 --eval 2 for a quick check that everything works.

Run the LookAtMyQuant 2 recipe on Qwen3.5-4B

Each step is a named job; python run_batch.py --list prints its command. The jobs need Qwen3.5-4B in models/Qwen3.5-4B on the volume and the text mix (modal run --detach modal_fetch.py --text). Every file they make goes to lm2/ on the volume.

modal run --detach modal_app.py --jobs lm2Text
modal run --detach modal_app.py --jobs lm2Calibration,lm2Solutions
modal run --detach modal_app.py --jobs lm2RowImportance
modal run --detach modal_app.py --jobs lm2Build
modal run --detach modal_app.py --jobs lm2Finetune
modal run --detach modal_app.py --jobs lm2Math,lm2Math216,lm2TextKL
Job Script What it does Our run
lm2Text other_text.py The original answers science, code, instruction and tool prompts, and MATH and GSM8K training problems. This also downloads MATH
lm2Calibration math_calibration.py The calibration set: the original's greedy solutions to 384 MATH training problems, in 2,048-token windows 15 minutes, H100
lm2Solutions checked_solutions.py The math text the fine-tuning distils on: solutions to MATH problems and to math_bench.py problems from another seed, with wrong calculations corrected and only right answers kept 33 minutes, H100
lm2RowImportance row_importance.py Each output row's Fisher information at digit-predicting positions 1 minute, H100
lm2Build quantize.py Post-training quantization: trellis codes along rows, digit tokens weighted 10× in the Hessians, QEP at α = 0.5, bits per row from the row plan, e-means codebooks 37 minutes, H100
lm2Finetune finetune.py 4,000 steps of distillation on latent weights pulled toward their codes, with every layer re-quantized once from the original weights 2.7 hours, B200
lm2Math, lm2Math216 math_eval.py The 540-problem benchmark and a second set of 216, for the original, Bonsai, the build and the fine-tuned build 20 minutes a model, H100
lm2TextKL text_kl.py KL from the original on WikiText-2 and on the text mix's 13 sources 1 minute a model, H100

lm2BuildSmoke, lm2FinetuneSmoke and lm2MathSmoke run the same code on two layers, 60 steps and 36 problems, in a few minutes each.

The row plan. lm2Build reads results/compiler/rows/q35_rowplan_1p2GB.json, which gives 1 to 4 bits to each of 1,520 row groups. row_allocation.py made it. Its build-control command builds and packs a control with a fixed split of rows, prepare-rows allocates rows inside the control's packed bytes with rowgroup_alloc.py, and build-rows builds under the plan and checks the packed size against it.

The codebooks. The four e-means codebooks the build decodes with are in cache/codes/. --trellis-fit lloyd gives the earlier ones, and a plan made before the change keeps them unless the flag says otherwise.

Recent equal-byte recipe improvements. Two zero-byte additions are available in the compiler and fine-tuning scripts:

  • Softmax-Fisher token table ranking (--embed-order sfisher-mix in compiler.py measure and quantize.py). Ranks tied embedding/output buckets by a 50/50 blend of output Softmax-Fisher E[p_v (1 - p_v)] and corpus frequency (and untied output heads by Softmax-Fisher alone).
  • Mid-training equal-byte row reallocation (--realloc-at 1000 in finetune.py). Paired with --rebuild-at 1000, measures each layer's continuous-vs-stored proximal KL gap KL(all P) - KL(layer = W) to shift bits toward deep unabsorbed layers while keeping exact file size (--realloc-max-delta 1). Combined with sfisher-mix on Qwen3.5-4B at identical 1.23 GB (2.297 bpp), WikiText-2 KL fell from 0.425 to 0.387 (−9.0%) and 13-source KL from 0.447 to 0.378 (−15.5%, improving all 13 sources).

Where these jobs differ from our run. Our GSM8K solutions were written earlier, with thinking always off. Our text KL on 13 sources used 52 windows picked from the text mix by a separate tool; --sources mix takes the mix's own evaluation windows, on which our file scores 0.44 where the page reports 0.45.

Large models run on Modal, one GPU per job

run_batch.py names every job, and modal_app.py runs them. modal_fetch.py downloads models and the text mix used for calibration and evaluation.

modal run modal_app.py::setup
modal run --detach modal_fetch.py --text
modal run --detach modal_fetch.py --models google/gemma-4-E2B-it
modal run --detach modal_app.py --jobs ccMG4E2Noise,ccMG4E2Spot,ccMG4E2EmbKv

The runs behind the site used these machines, each with 8 CPU cores:

Model GPU Time
SmolLM2-360M L40S About 50 minutes to measure, in 9 parallel jobs
Gemma 4 E2B, measuring H100 7–26 minutes per job, in 4 jobs
Gemma 4 E2B, building a plan H100 28–58 minutes per plan

gguf_compiler.py makes plans out of llama.cpp's own tensor types, so the result runs in llama.cpp as it is. public_eval.py scores public quantizations the same way as our plans. Both run inside the image in modal_gguf.py, which builds llama.cpp with CUDA.

The Apple Silicon runtime reads Lloyd–Max and trellis plans

quantize.py --export <folder> writes a plan in the format runtime_mlx/ reads. A plan with trellis codes also needs --trellis-rows 16,8, which runs each trellis path along a row of its matrix, so that decoding an entry reads only that row. On Apple silicon, pip install . installs mlx and mlx-lm; requirements.txt holds the PyTorch compiler dependencies.

On Gemma 4 E2B at 2.5 GB, the trellis plan has 26% lower KL than the Lloyd–Max plan and decodes about 22% slower. runtime_mlx/test_trellis_gen.py and runtime_mlx/test_trellis.py check the trellis kernels against the matrices the quantizer built.

python runtime_mlx/bench.py lamq path/to/export

A drafter makes the 1.2 GB file generate 1.5 to 2 times faster on Apple silicon

runtime_mlx/fast_q35.py decodes the packed 1.2 GB Qwen3.5-4B file one token at a time, straight from its trellis codes. runtime_mlx/drafter_q35.py adds speculative decoding. A small drafter proposes the seven tokens after the model's latest one in a single pass. The model then checks all eight positions in one pass over its coded weights (runtime_mlx/block_q35.py) and keeps the proposals that match its own choice, so the text is exactly its own greedy text.

On an M5 Max, over 30 held-out prompts of up to 256 tokens, generation with the drafter was 2.0 times as fast: 176 tokens a second against 88, timed in alternation in one process on 2026-11-11. A check kept 4.3 tokens on average. Over eight everyday prompts it was 1.5 times as fast. The gain follows how predictable the text is: 2.5 times on algebra, 2.0 on code, 1.2 on chat and 1.05 on a story, and one of the 30 held-out prompts ran slower with the drafter. The text matched plain greedy decoding on every prompt. These are speeds after the first token; reading the prompt takes about 0.1 s either way.

Two later changes are in this code. Each was measured against the version before it on 40 paired generations: proposing from the 96,033 most common tokens was 6.0% faster, and picking the winning token inside the packed product was 5.3% faster. Linear mode also enables self-calibrating adaptive fallback by default (adaptive=True; pass --no-adaptive to disable): when rolling acceptance drops below the measured break-even ratio of drafted-check latency to serial-step latency (accounting for cache flush and drafter context replay), it pauses drafting for short exact serial bursts and resumes once acceptance recovers, preserving bit-exact greedy parity while avoiding slowdowns on low-acceptance prose.

The drafter is a DSpine model, trained with SpecForge from the published DFlash drafter for Qwen3.5-4B on the 1.2 GB file's own greedy answers. modal_drafter.py runs the training as one Modal job, and it cost $42. On 300 held-out prompts the trained drafter gets 4.65 tokens per check, against 4.30 for the stock DFlash drafter.

pack_drafter.py stores the drafter at 4 bits a weight in the build's own code, with no calibration data: 464 MB against 1.83 GB at 16 bits. On 60 held-out prompts the 4-bit drafter kept 4.35 tokens per check against 4.38, and the text was the same. drafter_q35.py loads either form and writes the packed one out dense as it loads. The 4-bit drafter is the lm2-drafter-4bit release. It runs beside the packed 1.2 GB file, the lm2-qwen35-4b-1.2gb release.

gh release download lm2-qwen35-4b-1.2gb --repo ShinMegamiBoson/lookatmyquant -D q35-1.2gb
gh release download lm2-drafter-4bit --repo ShinMegamiBoson/lookatmyquant -D drafter-4bit
python runtime_mlx/bench_drafted.py q35-1.2gb drafter-4bit

The benchmark defaults to linear verification. Use --mode chat-fork to try a second candidate at an ambiguous early position, or --mode copy-wide for known contiguous copies. Copy mode uses the source cursor and tunes the gate/up and down projections for 16-slot checks. Both modes verify all emitted tokens with the packed target. To benchmark the chat fork, run:

python runtime_mlx/bench_drafted.py q35-1.2gb drafter-4bit --mode chat-fork --prompts chat

For a copy benchmark, pass --mode copy-wide --heldout path/to/copy-prompts.json. The JSON entries carry source, prompt_len, and input_ids from the packed model's tokenizer.

The checks, and the packer for a drafter of your own:

python runtime_mlx/test_fast_q35.py
LAMQ_Q35_PACKED=path/to/packed python runtime_mlx/test_block_q35.py
python runtime_mlx/check_drafter.py path/to/packed path/to/drafter
python runtime_mlx/bench_drafted.py path/to/packed path/to/drafter --heldout path/to/drafter/heldout/heldout.json --take 30
python pack_drafter.py path/to/drafter path/to/drafter-4bit

runtime_mlx/pack_dense.py writes the packed file from the fine-tuned build's dense weights, and runtime_mlx/modal_pack.py runs it on Modal. check_drafter.py compares the drafter in MLX with SpecForge's own model on reference blocks that drafter/reference.py writes.

Where everything is

Path What it holds
compiler.py Measure and allocate
compiler_arch.py How the compiler finds a model's layers, tables and stages, and the text mix
quantize.py Builds a program or a plan, then scores it
row_importance.py, rowgroup_alloc.py, row_allocation.py, compiler_artifact.py Bits per row: each row's importance, the allocation, the builds it compares, and the packed format that prices them
math_calibration.py, checked_solutions.py, other_text.py, calc_check.py, token_kinds.py The text the recipe calibrates and fine-tunes on, the checker for stated calculations, and the kind of token each position predicts
finetune.py, finetune_lib.py, fast_delta.py Fine-tuning that ends on the codes, and a faster linear-attention rule for Qwen3.5
math_bench.py, math_eval.py, text_kl.py The exact-answer math benchmark, its runner for the Qwen3.5 family and Bonsai, and KL from the original on text
gguf_compiler.py, public_eval.py, eval_tasks.py The llama.cpp route, public quantizations and task benchmarks
pyproject.toml, runtime_mlx/runtime.py, runtime_mlx/cli.py Installable Apple Silicon runtime package, unified load/Runtime Python API, and lamq CLI
lamq_export.py, runtime_mlx/ The export format and the Apple Silicon runtime
runtime_mlx/fast_q35.py, block_q35.py, block_argmax_q35.py, pack_dense.py, modal_pack.py The runtime for packed Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.8-27B files: one token at a time, a block of 8 or 16 tokens in one pass, and the packer
runtime_mlx/inkling/, runtime_mlx/test_inkling.py Apple Silicon MLX runtime, 4 KB SRAM ht2/ht3 Metal kernels, and 4-bit DSpark block-8 speculative drafter for packed Inkling-2-Mini models
runtime_mlx/drafter_q35.py, draft_vocab_q35.py, convert_dspine.py, check_drafter.py, bench_drafted.py, drafter/, modal_drafter.py, pack_drafter.py Speculative decoding with a DSpine drafter, Tencent DSpine conversion, drafter training, and the drafter stored at 4 bits
opgraph/ The grammar: a model as a tensor network, and the rewrites and codes that act on it
run_completeness.py, make_report.py The check that nine published methods are reproduced exactly
analyze_compiler.py The tables of plan results
run_batch.py, modal_app.py, modal_gguf.py, modal_fetch.py Named jobs and the Modal runners
results/compiler/plans/, results/compiler/rows/ Every plan, and the row plan for Qwen3.5-4B at 1.2 GB
results/protocols/ The second math set of 216 problems, and the hashes of every question kept out of training text
cache/codes/ The e-means trellis codebooks at 1 to 4 bits
results/batch/, results/gguf/ The measurements and plan runs behind the site
results/COMPILER.md, results/COMPLETENESS.md Write-ups of the compiler on SmolLM2-360M and Qwen3.5-4B, and of the reproduction check
site/ The website. Run python3 -m http.server 8000 inside it, then visit http://localhost:8000
site2/ The LookAtMyQuant 2 page. It runs the same way
tests/ Tests of the grammar and the codes

The tests need SmolLM2-360M and WikiText-2

Each test file runs on its own from the repository root, and all seven finish in under a minute.

python tests/test_frame.py
python tests/test_grammar.py
python tests/test_codes.py
python tests/test_elements.py
python tests/test_nested.py
python tests/test_rowgroup_alloc.py
python tests/test_reallocation.py

runtime_mlx/test_core.py checks the runtime against the quantizer's math. Run python runtime_mlx/make_ref.py first, which writes 1.6 GB of reference files.

runtime_mlx/test_fast_q35.py and runtime_mlx/test_block_q35.py check the Qwen3.5 kernels against NumPy products of independently unpacked codes, with no model. When LAMQ_Q35_PACKED names a packed file, the second also checks a block of tokens against decoding them one at a time. When LAMQ_Q38_PACKED names the packed Qwen3.8-27B file, it runs the same checks on a model whose output head is stored apart from its embedding.

What this repository leaves out

  • Model weights. Everything downloads from Hugging Face. The Qwen3.5-4B jobs expect that model in models/Qwen3.5-4B on the volume.
  • Benchmark copies. eval_tasks.py downloads its benchmarks. On an offline machine it reads exported copies from data/bench/, which are not here. The Modal images run offline, so cache the benchmarks on the volume first.
  • The script that assembled site/data.json. It was a set of one-off steps. The source numbers are all in results/.
  • LookAtMyQuant 2's dense weights and result files. The 1.2 GB file is a release in the packed format. The dense weights the benchmarks ran on are not published, and neither are the per-problem results behind site2/data.json or the script that writes the page's numbers from them.
  • The drafter at 16 bits. The drafter as trained is 1.8 GB and is not published. The 4-bit one is a release file, and modal_drafter.py trains it.

item.title: PostgreSQL Extensions in Go (108 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://jespino.github.io/gopgext/, See on Hacker News

gopgext builds PostgreSQL extensions from plain Go code, using TinyGo. Mark a function with //gopgext:function and it becomes a SQL function: gopgext writes the C glue, the install script and the control file.

Experimentalgopgext is experimental. Don’t use it in production: a bug in the generated code or the Go runtime runs inside the server, where it can crash it or corrupt data, and the API and generated SQL may change without notice.

Just Go

A project is plain Go files. The standard library works: fmt, regexp, encoding/json, crypto/*, maps, generics, iterators, defer/recover.

Types map to SQL

Strings, numbers, arrays, NULLs, sets, rows, timestamps, UUIDs and JSON map to SQL types. Define your own data types and composite types in Go.

Queries and errors

Run SQL through SPI, return errors with SQLSTATE codes, log, read settings and stay responsive to query cancellation.

Beyond functions

Write triggers, aggregates, GiST, GIN, SP-GiST and BRIN operator classes, index access methods, foreign data wrappers and query hooks.

Proven on contrib

Ports of PostgreSQL’s contrib modules (pgcrypto, hstore, pg_stat_statements, cube, …) pass upstream’s regression tests.

Safe coexistence

Several Go extensions load in one backend. PostgreSQL errors never unwind through Go frames, and results are copied into PostgreSQL memory.

Hello, world#

package main

import (
	"strings"

	"gopgext/pg"
)

// Hello returns a greeting for name.
//
//gopgext:function immutable parallel=safe
func Hello(name string) string {
	return "Hello, " + name + "!"
}

// Shout upper-cases s. An empty string raises an error.
//
//gopgext:function immutable parallel=safe
func Shout(s string) (string, error) {
	if s == "" {
		return "", pg.Errorf(pg.CodeInvalidParameterValue, "nothing to shout")
	}
	return strings.ToUpper(s) + "!", nil
}

func main() {} // runs once per backend, when PostgreSQL loads the library

gopgext init hello       # creates hello/go.mod and hello/main.go
gopgext install hello    # builds hello.so, hello.control, hello--1.0.sql and installs them
psql -c 'CREATE EXTENSION hello' -c "SELECT hello('world')"
#     hello
# ---------------
#  Hello, world!

The tutorial walks through it step by step.

A sibling project#

gopgext uses the same approach as gokm, which builds Linux kernel modules from Go: a custom TinyGo target and runtime layer for the host, a C runtime compiled by the host’s own build system (PGXS here, kbuild there), and generated glue.

item.title: Show HN: Zero C# – C# without a runtime or GC (116 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://onurgumus.github.io/zero-csharp/index.html, See on Hacker News

A fork of bflat compiles C# straight to a small native program: no .NET runtime, no garbage collector, nothing to install where it runs.

You keep C#'s syntax, type checking and generics. Memory comes from arenas you free all at once, and a small library gives you strings, collections, input and output on those terms. The same source runs on Linux, macOS and Windows, on WebAssembly, and on DOS on a 386.

// Read into a stack buffer: nothing allocated per answer.
Span<char> buffer = stackalloc char[32];

Out.Write($"Q{i}: {a} + {b} = ");
int length = In.ReadLine(buffer);

// Kept until the end, so it goes into an arena.
mistakes.Add(Str.Format(keep,
    $"{a} + {b} = {a + b}, not {value}"));

From the quiz the tutorial builds, step by step.

The language stays, the runtime goes

The compiler still checks everything it checks in .NET. What's missing is what a runtime would do while your program runs.

You keep

  • C# 15Unions, extension members and the new memory safety rules.
  • Real genericsA specialized copy for each type, and static abstract members.
  • Interfaces and virtual methodsDefault interface methods, casts, is and as.
  • Records, tuples, anonymous typesValue equality, with, and the generated ToString.
  • Lambdas and queriesWhere, Select and GroupBy, from a small library instead of LINQ.
  • ThreadsParallel.For runs a loop on every core.

You do without

  • Garbage collectorArenas free their memory all at once, when you say.
  • .NET runtimeHello world is 11 KB on Windows and 40 KB on Linux, with nothing to install.
  • Catching exceptionsthrow ends the program. Return errors as unions.
  • Reflection and asyncA type can be compared, but it has no name.

One program, five machines

The hello-world sample, unchanged, built for each target. Each build is checked by the same test suite, which requires the same output everywhere.

$ ./build.sh Minimal
$ ./run.sh Minimal
Hello from zero-mode!
$ wc -c bin/Minimal
39848 bin/Minimal

Linux, x64 or arm64

A native program that needs only the C library. On macOS it builds and runs in a container.

$ ./build.sh --mac Minimal
$ bin/mac/Minimal
Hello from zero-mode!
$ wc -c bin/mac/Minimal
64728 bin/mac/Minimal

macOS on Apple Silicon

A native Mac program: bflat compiles it, the Mac's own clang links it. No container to run it.

$ ./build.sh --win Minimal
$ ./run.sh --win Minimal
Hello from zero-mode!
$ wc -c bin/win/Minimal.exe
10752 bin/win/Minimal.exe

Windows x64

A console program on Windows' own C library, built from Linux or macOS. Tested under Wine.

$ ./build.sh --wasm Minimal
$ ./run.sh --wasm Minimal
Hello from zero-mode!
$ wc -c bin/wasm/Minimal.wasm
15833 bin/wasm/Minimal.wasm

WebAssembly

A WASI module, through NativeAOT-LLVM. Runs under wasmtime.

C:\>D:
D:\>PROGRAM
Hello from zero-mode!

D:\>DIR PROGRAM.EXE
PROGRAM  EXE     16,384

D:\>

DOS on a 386

The same bitcode compiled for a 386, run by the HX DOS extender. Tested on Bochs's i386 model.

What's different, and what you get

Without a runtime, a few things work differently. Each has a page that explains why and what to do instead.

  • Memory is yours to free

    There is no garbage collector, so new is never freed. Arenas hand out memory and free it all at once, one per lifetime.

    Memory without a garbage collector

  • Text without throwaway strings

    Out.Line($"...") formats straight into the output buffer, and In.ReadLine reads into a span. Strings that must last go into an arena.

    Strings without a garbage collector

  • Collections that live in arenas

    List, Dict, and their versions for references and string keys, all handles into an arena.

    Choose a collection

  • C# 15, with the safety rules on

    Every program compiles under the updated memory safety rules: creating a pointer is safe, reading through one is marked and explained.

    The memory safety rules

Where to start

If you're new to it, these four pages take you from nothing to an interactive program.

  1. Install

    With dotnet on Linux, or from the repository for every target.

  2. Your first program

    Build it, run it, see how small it is.

  3. Run it on DOS

    The same program under FreeDOS, in an emulator.

  4. The tutorial

    A quiz: output, input, bad input, arenas.

Looking for something specific? The task guides answer one question each, and the reference lists every type in the library.

item.title: Lean Verification of the Riemann Hypothesis - Joint statement by... (745 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://leanprover-community.github.io/blog/posts/riemann-hypothesis/, See on Hacker News

Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis

Joint statement by the Lean and Mathlib communities, endorsed by the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative.

On November 20, 2026, Levent Alpöge released a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis as a Lean library comprising 17 million lines of code.

We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement.

Our rationale is outlined below.

The codebase depends directly only on Mathlib. Over the past day, the Lean and Mathlib communities have rallied to verify the proof's correctness. We hereby certify that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis are correct. The four criteria in https://xenaproject.wordpress.com/2026/11/12/and-the-proof-is-checked-in-lean/ are all satisfied.

  1. The statement of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct. This statement is part of Mathlib: RiemannHypothesis and has been carefully vetted by experts in Lean and number theory.
  2. Alpöge’s library compiles correctly. By now, dozens of people have reported correct compilation of the codebase, reproducing the same raw proof export file. The library compiles without errors or build failures.
  3. The code proves the correct statement. Crucially, the community has added a file that isolates the statement of the Riemann Hypothesis and imports only Mathlib. That statement was compared against the theorem proved by Alpöge using two independent tools (comparator and con-leche –compare), both confirming that the theorem proved in Alpöge’s library is exactly Mathlib’s statement of the Riemann Hypothesis.
  4. The Lean proof is valid. The exported raw proof has been checked by several proof checkers, including Lean’s official kernel, the con-leche and con-ron checkers, and several independent checkers contributed by third parties and implemented in different programming languages. The checkers con-leche and con-ron come with a formal proof, relative to set theory, that they cannot accept a false proof, thus addressing concerns that Lean’s logic itself might have flaws that the proof could exploit. An extensive overview is available at https://math.mit.edu/~drew/grh/. These checks ran on an inert export of the proof, out of reach of hypothetical malicious code in the Lean proof sources.

Thanks are owed to everyone in the community who provided resources for the verification.

We look forward to all the activity in the mathematical community that will help explain the new ideas in this proof.

We introduce SimpleBench, a multiple-choice text benchmark for LLMs where individuals with unspecialized (high school) knowledge outperform SOTA models. SimpleBench includes over 200 questions covering spatio-temporal reasoning, social intelligence, and what we call linguistic adversarial robustness (or trick questions). For the vast majority of text-based benchmarks LLMs outperform a non-specialized human, and increasingly, exceed expert human performance. However, on SimpleBench, a non-specialized human baseline is 83.7%, based on our small sample of nine participants,

outperforming every tested LLM, including today's top model, Claude Fable, which scored 81.9%

. While we expect model performance to improve over time, the results of SimpleBench confirm that the memorized knowledge, and approximate reasoning retrieval, utilized by frontier LLMs is not always enough to answer basic questions just yet.

item.title: My Monitor Was Cutting My Download Speed by 75% (438 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://blog.tymscar.com/posts/studiodisplayethernet/, See on Hacker News

Somehow I am one of those few very lucky people to have the opportunity of owning a 2.5 gig symmetrical line for my internet. But one day, when I wanted to brag to my equally nerdy friends, shock and horror: 600 Mbps down? Luckily my upload speed was still 2.4 Gbps, so I didn’t lose all my bragging rights, but that’s weird, right? If anything, you’d expect the opposite!

My ISP is pretty cool. It’s run by this one guy (Hey Keith!), and I know I can always message them and they respond promptly, as they did this time. We tried to run through a few debugging steps, they checked on their end, and everything was normal. I tried my work laptop too, same speed.

I didn’t have time for debugging, because I needed to travel 2000 km to the other side of the continent for a family emergency.

But as soon as I got back, I got curious again. What could it be? In retrospect, I now know when it started: when I moved all my connections onto my Studio Display XDR. I wanted to have a one-cable setup, and the monitor offered me that. I’ve had it for half a year now, and I don’t think I’ve ever run a speed test through it. 600 Mbps was more than fast enough for me to never realise I wasn’t getting three quarters of the speed I was paying for 🤦

The setup#

  • MacBook Pro M3 Pro
  • 2026 Studio Display XDR, with everything plugged into it so switching laptops is one cable
  • UGREEN USB-C to 2.5G Ethernet adapter, plugged into the display
  • UniFi Dream Router 7, the same one from my WiFi 7 debugging post

What I thought was interesting#

Pings to other wired computers during a download would fail 10% of the time over Ethernet through the adapter plugged into my screen, and 0% of the time over Wi-Fi. What made it stranger was that there were no dropped frame errors in macOS’s logs at all. This was the big hint for me: the adapter was dropping them before the computer could know.

I then plugged the adapter straight into my Mac instead of the monitor, and ran an iperf3 server on my UDR 7: 2.3 Gbps. So the cable, the router and the adapter are all fine? What about fast.com? Perfect speeds there too! 2.2 down and 2.3 up when connected straight in. As soon as I connected it to the display, it was back to 600 down again.

So it’s the display, right? Well, I would find out: sort of yes, sort of no, which is why I wanted to write this blog post. I couldn’t find anything online explaining the exact cause, and it’s quite a cool reason.

The driver and flow control#

The adapter uses a Realtek RTL8156B, which on macOS binds to Apple’s generic USB networking driver. But Realtek ship their own driver on their website, so I thought I’d give that a go! I installed it and, to my surprise, it almost doubled the download speed to 1.1 Gbps, but that was still nowhere close to 2.5. First hint that it couldn’t just be the monitor’s fault.

Then I tried flow control. I had never truly looked into this before, and I think it’s quite neat to know about if you were also ignorant of it like me. Basically, when a device receives Ethernet frames it can’t keep up with, it just drops them. With flow control (it’s something your router or switch has to support), it can send the sender a “pause” frame, and the sender then buffers the data on its side, instead of the receiver (the adapter in this case) on its side. I turned it on in my UniFi console and guess what, download jumped to around 2 Gbps, with upload still at full speed! Yay! Well, not so fast…

I don’t like it always being on, because it can add latency to other systems like my gaming PC. Can you work around it? For sure, you can disable it on those computers, but it’s janky, and it’s another thing I need to remember when my Sauerbraten game starts lagging. I need fewer things to remember, considering I am 30 in a couple of months. My memory is not what it used to be.

But the upload was always fine#

Yeah, isn’t that weird? First of all, it looks like the port can indeed do 2.5 in both directions. I already knew that, because I get much more than that from my external SSD through the monitor’s Thunderbolt port. So the issue is not the monitor again? But it has to be!

Well, I had another idea. How about I connect to my Linux box, which is also on 2.5, and send perfectly smooth UDP traffic at a fixed rate with flow control off? Then I can check the chip’s own counter of dropped frames:

SentLost behind the displayFrames/s reaching the Mac behind the displayLost direct on the Mac
1.46 Gbps0%123,8000%
1.75 Gbps0.05%148,6000%
1.94 Gbps0.1%165,0000%
2.03 Gbps2.7%168,0000%
2.12 Gbps7.2%168,0000%
2.20 Gbps10.5%168,0000.001%
2.28 Gbps13.5%168,0000.02%

So basically no drops whatsoever when connected straight to my Mac, but loads of drops after about 168k frames per second (roughly 2 Gbps). Remember that number. That number comes from the adapter’s own counters: however much I sent, the number of frames it managed to hand over to the Mac each second flattened out at about 168,000, and everything above that was dropped.

Why did this not happen on my SSD? What was the only difference I could find? Bursts!

When the Mac reads data from a USB 3 device, the device sends some packets, then has to wait for the Mac to say “lgtm, send more!”. The SSD enclosure sends 16 packets before needing a go-ahead message back. The RTL8156B in my Ethernet adapter sends 4.

Here is a diagram of my best understanding of why this is an issue. I made this diagram 100 times, and I think I can probably improve it more, but if it helps you understand the issue, I have done my job.

As you can see, the speed of packets coming into the adapter is 2.5 Gbps. That’s what the router pushes in. The speed going out is around 2 Gbps. The reason is that if you add up the average time it takes to get the go-ahead through my monitor’s hub, which is around 7.6 µs, to the average time it takes to send 4 KB, around 8.2 µs, you can find what the maximum speed is.

Well, if the speed of the drain from my adapter to my Mac is half a gig slower than the speed of the input, then you can imagine the buffer getting filled more and more until it overflows. Those are dropped packets, which result in a hard backoff when the router resends them, so you drop loads in speed. And that’s the reason for all of this.

OK, well, what now?#

I have a cupboard full of USB-C Ethernet adapters. Don’t ask.

The problem is they’re all 1 gig adapters, so any of the tests I made would not tell me anything, because the issues don’t start at 1 gig. They start at around 2… If I run my 2.5 gig adapter at 1 gig speeds, I get 1 gig downloads with the official driver. If I run it at 1.5, I get 1.5. If I run it at 2, well, I get 1…

So I thought I would do what any human would do, and I spent more money on a new adapter. Another UGREEN, but this time it’s one that promises 5 Gbps and uses the RTL8157 chip instead: UGREEN 5G USB-C Ethernet adapter. My reasoning was that if this one could get me better speeds, it would help me understand how. And that it did!

With this adapter, I dropped 0 frames:

SentFrames/s reaching the MacDropped by the adapter
1.5 Gbps124k0
1.9 Gbps157k0
2.1 Gbps173k0
2.3 Gbps187k0
2.4 Gbps194k0

Why? Well, looking through what each adapter tells me about itself:

$ python3 -c "import usb.core; e = usb.core.find(idVendor=0x0bda)[0][(0,0)][0]; print('packet size', e.wMaxPacketSize, 'bMaxBurst', e.extra_descriptors[2])"

# old adapter (RTL8156B)
packet size 1024 bMaxBurst 3

# new adapter (RTL8157)
packet size 1024 bMaxBurst 7

# bMaxBurst counts the packets after the first one, so 3 means 4 packets and 7 means 8

I can see that instead of sending 4 1 KB packets per burst, it would send 8! And the speed of the link was also 2x faster, so those 8 KB would go 2x faster to the Mac. That means the time spent was 8 times lower to send the same data, and while the wait for the go-ahead was identical, the theoretical speed from the adapter to the Mac, including the wait for the go-ahead, was a maximum of 4.5 Gbps. That’s much bigger than the 2.5 coming into the adapter, so the buffer would never fill up, packets would never drop and everything was great, even if the “go-ahead” response was still much slower than when connected directly to the Mac.

Final thoughts#

I think the big takeaway from this is that all the things you think are quite easy to understand, such as transfer speeds, have so many cool intricacies that it’s worth diving deep every so often. Who would’ve thought that the speed of the link between the adapter and the Mac was defined not only by the link speed itself in Gbps, but also by the time it took your Mac to reply, by the amount of packets, by the speed of those packets, by the number of packets in a burst, and by the size of those packets?

See you next time, when I will spend just as much time on another trivial thing that we can all learn from!

item.title: RCE in Gnupg (221 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://lists.gnupg.org/pipermail/gnupg-announce/2026q4/000517.html, See on Hacker News

Werner Koch wk at gnupg.org

Hello!

We are pleased to announce the availability of a new GPGME release:
version 2.3.1.  This version fixes a *critical security bug* found in
all prior versions.  We also release a new Gpg4win versions and and
GnuPG Desktop and GnuPG VS-Desktop versions which all make use of GPGME.


Description
===========

By using an OpenPGP key containing a crafted very long user id it is
possible to trigger a double free.  This double free can be used
exfiltrate data from applications by sending for example signed data.
Exploiting this bug to mount an Remote Code Execution attack (RCE) can't
be ruled out.  Thus an immediate update is highly suggested.

Our internal ID is T8557 (https://static.dev.gnupg.org/T8557)
The CVE-id is CVE-2026-129975.

This vulnerability was discovered by Johan Carlsson and we were informed
by GitLab on 2026-11-12.  Initially we set 2026-11-25 for a coordinated
disclosure; due to the new Ruby2Shell bug GitLab had to update earlier
and thus we also disclosed the GPGME bug on 2026-11-20.

The root cause for this bug are two GPGME internal functions to read the
status lines and key listings from gpg.  Initially a buffer of 1024
bytes is allocated which is reallocated if more space is required.  When
reallocating the pointer to the new buffer is used by the function but
it is only assigned back to the context object at the end of the
function.  Thus if the function returns early due to an read error or
other events the context is not updated and keeps the stale pointer to
the freed memory.  Eventually the context is released and the memory
freed a second time.  Due to other allocations in between the common
double free checks of memory allocators may not be triggered.


Impact
======

All software using a GPGME version prior to 2.3.0 either as shared
libary, DLL, or statically linked is affected.  Examples of software
using GPGME are

 - Gpg4win
 - GnuPG Desktop
 - GnuPG VS-Desktop
 - Most mail clients
 - Many XMPP clients
 - Samba
 - Flatpack


Solution
========

Please update your GPGME shared library to version 2.3.1.  If you need a
DLL you may take it from from the updated Gpg4win version.

For statically linked binaries remmeber to build them against GPGME
2.3.1.

If for some reasons GPGME can't be updated, you may patch your GPGME
version using the attached patch which likley applies cleanly even to
very old versions.

There is no need to udpate GPGMEPP or GPGMEQT.


Noteworthy changes in version 2.3.1 (2026-11-19)
================================================
         [compared to version 2.2.0]

 * New constants GPGME_PK_MLKEM, GPGME_PK_MLDSA, and GPGME_PK_DLTHM.
   Add mappings for algos used bei backends.   [rMa85fa49236]

 * Fix a double free in the status line read code.
   [T8557,CVE-2026-129975]

 * Interface changes relative to the 2.2.0 release:
 ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
 GPGME_PK_DLTHM                NEW.
 GPGME_PK_MLKEM                NEW.
 GPGME_PK_MLDSA                NEW.

 Release-info: https://dev.gnupg.org/T8427


Getting the Software
====================

Please follow the instructions found at <https://gnupg.org/download/> or
read on:

The GPGME source code compressed using BZIP2 and its OpenPGP signature
are available here:

 https://gnupg.org/ftp/gcrypt/gpgme/gpgme-2.3.1.tar.bz2 (1393k)

A sufficient patch to solve the security bug for older versions is
attached.   Note that version 2.3.0 was never publicly available.

===============

Windows Installer

reader has also been released.  Head over to https://gpg4win.org/

item.description:
URL: http://ricapar.net/ClawDOS/, See on Hacker News

Ricapar/ClawDOS

ClawDOS

An AI coding agent for DOS.
It runs on an IBM PC XT: an 8088 at 4.77 MHz, 640K of RAM, a CGA card.

A (real) human’s note:

Backstory: The IBM PC was my first computer. Rather, it was my parents’ first personal computer that I got to use at a very early age.

It was already obsolete by the time I was old enough to use it, but at 5 years old it was a magical device that I could make do different things depending on what I typed.

I learned how to type and use DOS so that I could launch some early “Learn the Alphabet” games that my mom had bought me. I learned some elementary-level use of BASIC, but at the time that didn’t progress much further than making some number guessing games and other small projects.

From there, many years passed but I still have some of the original parts of that PC. I have a collection of vintage machines that mean something to me, with my fully maxed-out IBM PC 5160 being the centerpiece of my collection. It still has a working 20 MB hard drive, but that’s disconnected in favor of a PicoMEM that lets me emulate a hard drive off of an SD card, making experimentation and play much easier.

Old, meet new. New, meet old: I love intersections of old and new technology. What better way to cross the two than building an AI coding agent to run on DOS on original hardware?

And of course, what better to build it than an AI coding agent?

I (read: Claude) built this for my own entertainment. I wanted to see how far I could push an AI coding agent to build something given out of the (modern) norm of constraints. Also, can that something it built then build other somethings? 100% of this repo is written by Claude, with the exception of the text within this box.

As explained in more detail below, the harness runs on the native OS and hardware and relies on a “bridge” PC in order to handle TLS, which would’ve been more than what an 8088 could handle.

Type CLAWDOS at the C:\> prompt and talk to Claude. It reads and edits the files on your disk, writes programs, compiles them with Turbo C, runs them and looks at what they draw on the screen. It keeps notes between conversations and picks up where it left off.

The whole harness runs on the PC. HARNESS.EXE is a 176 KB DOS program that speaks the Claude Messages API itself: it writes the requests, parses the streamed reply, runs the tools and keeps every conversation on its own disk. The 8088 does everything but TLS.

See it work

Every screen below comes from a 5160 at 4.77 MHz, emulated in 86Box. The conversations are with the live API.

From a sentence to a running program

One message: “Write PRIMES.C: print the primes below 100. Compile it with Turbo C and run it.” ClawDOS reads its guide to the compilers on this machine, writes the source, then compiles, links and runs it in a single tool call. The answer is on the screen 64 seconds after Enter, 26 of them spent compiling, linking and running.

The compiler gets the machine to itself. For a build, ClawDOS saves its state and leaves memory, Turbo C runs with about 450K free, and the harness comes back on the same conversation with the program’s output in hand.

WarGames, written on the XT

ClawDOS wrote this tribute to the 1983 film on the PC itself: a vector world map, missiles arcing over the pole, a tic-tac-toe endgame, and a score for the PC speaker or an AdLib card. Five files of Turbo C, 15 KB of source, a WG.EXE under 10 KB.

Here it is running on the real 5160, filmed off its IBM monitor:


▶ Watch the WarGames demo on YouTube

It remembers

Start a new conversation and “your WarGames demo” is all it needs. ClawDOS opens the note it saved in C:\MEMORY, finds the latest build, and recalls the palette trick the war scene plays on the CGA.

It sees the screen

That Run call asked for a screenshot 25 seconds in. A timer-interrupt hook copies the CGA’s video memory at that moment, the 8088 encodes it as a PNG, and the picture goes to Claude with the tool result. This is the file the PC made, 320x200 in four colours, 16 KB:

And this is what Claude made of it:

An agent at work

Asked to make the demo exit on its own, ClawDOS goes looking. It searches the sources for the keyboard wait, reads the file, says what it found and edits one line. Each tool call shows in the transcript with its result, and between them Claude says what it is about to do.

It plays

Text art in sixteen colours, straight into the transcript, and music on the PC speaker in GW-BASIC’s PLAY language.

The harness

A chat screen built for the CGA. Replies stream onto the screen as they arrive, word-wrapped at 80 columns in code page 437. Writes are timed to the retrace, so there is no snow. The transcript scrolls in hardware through the CRTC start address, with PgUp and PgDn to go back. The spinner and its seconds run from the timer interrupt and keep moving while the PC is busy.

Eighteen tools. Claude works on the machine through these:

Tools What they do
sysinfo, dir, read, search Look at the system, list directories, read files as text or hex, find text across files
write, edit, delete, mkdir, rename Create and change files; edit replaces one piece of a file in place
run Run DOS programs and batch files and read back what they printed, up to twelve commands in a call, with a screenshot on request
peek, poke, port Read and write memory and I/O ports
play, textart PC speaker music and coloured CP437 art
memory_list, memory_read, memory_write Its own notes, kept in C:\MEMORY

A development kit on the disk. Two assemblers (TINYASM and WASM), Bruce’s C, GW-BASIC and the lDebug debugger, plus Turbo C 2.0, installed from your own floppy images in external/. All of them are proven on the 8088, and ClawDOS knows how to drive each one.

Memories and skills. Memories are what ClawDOS learns on your PC: what you built together, what worked, what you like. Skills are guides that ship with it, such as the dev tools and CGA demo effects. Both are plain text files on the disk, listed in every conversation’s system prompt and read when they fit the task. F4 browses the memories:

Safe mode. On by default. Anything that changes a file, memory or a port asks Allow ...? (y/n) first. F3 turns it off.

Conversations that last. Every chat is a file on the disk in the API’s own message format. F6 lists them, Enter reopens one, and your next message carries it on. A chat cut off by the power switch reopens too.

Any model, mid-conversation. /model lists the providers in CLAWDOS.CFG and switches between them and their models without losing the conversation. F5 sets how hard Claude thinks, from low to max. Any host that speaks the Messages API works.

Easy on a slow link. The system prompt and tools are cached by the API. After a conversation’s first request the PC uploads only what is new, so a tool result goes up in about 500 bytes. A dropped connection or an overloaded API is retried, and the turn carries on.

A flight recorder. CLAWDOS.LOG has a line for every round: time to first token, upload size and time, tokens in and out, cache reads.

api anthropic claude-opus-5-5 round=1 ttft=2750 total=4015 up=165 len=1784 stop=tool_use in=2 out=221 cr=5543 cw=739 th=cont
relaunch: program 61.5 s, CLAWDOS away 82.3 s

Under the hood

flowchart LR
    subgraph DOS["IBM PC XT (8088, 640K, CGA)"]
        direction TB
        subgraph APP["HARNESS.EXE"]
            direction TB
            UI["Chat screen"]
            LOOP["Agent loop<br/>Messages API requests, SSE and JSON,<br/>history on disk"]
            TOOLS["Tools<br/>files, search, DOS programs, screenshots,<br/>memory and ports, speaker"]
        end
        NET["mTCP + packet driver"]
        APP <--> NET
    end

    TUNNEL["TLS tunnel<br/>copies bytes"]
    API["Claude Messages API"]

    NET <-->|"plain HTTP"| TUNNEL
    TUNNEL <-->|"HTTPS"| API
   
Machine IBM PC XT 5160: 8088 at 4.77 MHz, 640K, CGA. A PicoMEM card supplies the disk (an image on microSD), WiFi as an NE2000, EMS and a battery clock
Code 13,000 lines of C and C++, built with Open Watcom for the 8086 instruction set
Programs HARNESS.EXE, 176 KB, the whole harness. CLAWDOS.EXE, 29 KB, the launcher you type
System FreeDOS 1.4 with mTCP for TCP/IP
API The Claude Messages API, streamed: tool use, images, prompt caching, message threads
TLS A tunnel on another machine, tunnel/tunnel.py, socat or stunnel. It copies bytes between a plain port and api.anthropic.com:443. It can also hold the API key, so the key never touches the PC’s disk
Memory A program ClawDOS runs gets 200K beside the harness, or 450K when the harness steps out
Tests 31 boot tests in DOSBox-X against a mock API, unit tests that run on DOS, and runs on 86Box’s 8088

docs/API.md has exactly what ClawDOS sends and what it expects back.

Run it

You need a Mac or a Windows PC with Python 3, and an Anthropic API key. On Windows the command is python.

python3 scripts/setup-tools.py          # fetch the compilers, FreeDOS, mTCP and the emulators
echo ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-... > .env
python3 scripts/build.py                # build/CLAWDOS.IMG, a bootable disk
python3 tunnel/tunnel.py                # the TLS tunnel, on port 8443
python3 scripts/run86box.py             # boot an IBM PC XT

At the C:\> prompt, type CLAWDOS.

No key? python3 tunnel/mockapi.py plays the API offline: type CLAWDOS 10.0.2.2:18023 and send !help.

On a real PC: build with the address of the machine running the tunnel (python3 scripts/build.py --tunnel 192.168.1.10:8443), copy CLAWDOS.IMG to the PicoMEM’s microSD card, pick it as the hard disk in the PicoMEM’s menu, boot, and type CLAWDOS. Later builds update the card’s image in place and keep its memories and chats (python3 scripts/build.py --update /path/to/CLAWDOS.IMG).

At the keyboard

Key  
Enter Send
Esc Stop a reply, or clear the input
Up / Down Recall earlier messages
PgUp / PgDn Scroll back
F1 Help
F2 New chat
F3 Safe mode on or off
F4 Memories
F5 Effort: low, medium, high, xhigh, max
F6 Earlier chats
F10 Quit

/model, /chats, /memories, /new and /quit work from the input box. CLAWDOS -m "..." sends a message from the command line and -c NAME reopens a chat.

More

   
docs/MANUAL.md Setup in full, real hardware, the image updater, other providers, every setting
docs/API.md What ClawDOS sends to the API and expects back
docs/ROADMAP.md The plan, the benchmark and the memory map
Path What
src/harness/ HARNESS.EXE: the chat screen, the turn, the tools
src/clawdos/ CLAWDOS.EXE, the launcher
lib/ The pieces: screen, console, network and HTTP, the API request writer and stream parser, JSON, history, the tool executors, screenshots and the PNG encoder
tunnel/ The TLS tunnel and the mock Messages API
image/ What goes on the disk: the manifest, the system prompt, the tool schemas, the skills, the tests
scripts/ Build, disk image tools, the emulator runners and test harnesses
tests/unit/ DOSUNIT.EXE, the unit tests that run on DOS

License

ClawDOS is free software under the GNU General Public License, version 3 or (at your option) any later version: see LICENSE. HARNESS.EXE links mTCP, which is GPLv3. The FreeDOS boot sector in src/boot/freedos is vendored unmodified under its own GPLv2-or-later license (its COPYING). Disk images you build hold other people’s software (FreeDOS, mTCP, and Turbo C from your own floppies): don’t redistribute an image with Turbo C on it.

ClawDOS stands on mTCP, FreeDOS, Open Watcom, the PicoMEM, 86Box and DOSBox-X.

item.title: Clojure will affect the way you think about programming (2017) (185 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://eli.thegreenplace.net/2017/clojure-the-perfect-language-to-expand-your-brain/, See on Hacker News

I sometimes get asked for recommendations of what programming language to "learn next". It's great that folks appreciate the fact that being exposed to several sufficiently different programming languages is an important step on the path to programming enlightenment. But it's also true that, given limited free time, the choice of which languages to learn is important. As the famous quote by Alan Perlis says:

A language that doesn't affect the way you think about programming, is not worth knowing.

In this post I want to explain why I think Clojure is a terrific language for this task. Whatever your background, it's almost guaranteed to affect the way you think about programming. It's a fairly new language (from 2007) that did a good job of collecting insights and paradigms from many existing languages and organizing them into a coherent whole. It's chock-full of great ideas. In other words, the perfect language to expand your brain.

It's a Lisp!

First and foremost, Clojure belongs to the Lisp family of languages, like Common Lisp, Scheme and Racket. Lisp is one of the oldest and still most important families of programming languages to be familiar with. Being a Lisp in this case means several things:

  • Clojure is a dynamic language. No matter where you stand on the static vs. dynamic typing debate, knowing languages in both camps is important. Clojure has a kind of optional typing, but in essence it's dynamic.
  • It promotes combinations of built-in data structures (lists, maps, vectors) over objects and has very good reasons for doing so.
  • It promotes programming with higher-order functions. Some built-in features like reducers and transducers rely heavily on composing higher order functions for transforming other functions.
  • It has uniform syntax with full Lisp-style macro support! This capability has proved to be very elusive for non-Lisp languages, and seeing some real macros in action is enlightening. Clojure has a whole Go-like CSP equivalent implemented using macros in core.async.
  • It encourages REPL-based development, where functionality is built and testsed gradually from the bottom up in an interactive terminal.

Importantly, Clojure is a very modern Lisp, with tons of libraries for tasks common in our day and age. It also builds upon important recent research in data structures, such as efficient persistent vectors, that only appeared in the 1990s or later. I've been dabbling with various Lisps for almost 15 years, and Clojure is the first Lisp I'd consider using in production.

I want the stress the importance of full Lisp-style macros once again. Lisp's (and Clojure's) uniform syntax and macros force us to think about the Meta-circular abstraction - there's just no way around it! We have to think of our code as data, and this has profound implications. Back in 2005, when I was still a programming neophyte, I faced a performance challenge for a data-decoding program I was hacking on in Perl. Having learned some Lisp, I had the insight of generating and evaluating new Perl code on the fly, which turned out to be key to the success of that program. I'm confident I could not have come up with that solution back then without being aware of the "Lisp way".

Pragmatism and hard-won experience

The designers of Clojure are extremely pragmatic, building upon decades of industry experience. I strongly recommend watching some YouTube videos of talks by leading Clojure developers. In particular, watch a few of the more popular talks by Rich Hickey - Clojure's original designer. The Alan Perlis quote mentioned above may be his most popular, but there's another I find at least as insightful:

Simplicity does not precede complexity, but follows it.

There's a certain quality in programmers I believe we can all recognize. It can only come from real, hard-won experience of building systems for many years and pondering about how to build such systems more effectively next time. Rich Hickey certainly belongs to this quality category - his talks are very insightful, and this philosophy reigns in the design and implementation of Clojure, as well as its (friendly and vibrant) community.

Sequences and laziness for powerful in-language data processing

Applications that process and extract useful bits of information from large datasets all look alike in many programming languages, at least to some extent. What we really want in many cases is SQL-like primitives built into our languages, but this is often challenging (.NET's LINQ is one example of a successful approach).

Clojure combines pervasive sequence protocols with persistent data structures and laziness to make this kind of task natural, using only built-in tools. Here's a realistic example of a function taken from the Clojure Applied book:

(defn revenue-by-department [carts]
  (->> (filter :settled? carts)
       (mapcat :line-items)
       (map line-summary)
       (group-by :dept)
       (reduce-kv dept-total)))

All the functions used here are built-ins, including the ->> macro. This code reads like SQL and it's efficient too. In fact, it can be made somewhat more efficient and even seamlessly parallelized using Reducers and Transducers.

The clojure.spec library provides a degree of type-safety for nested data structures. If you've ever written comments like "this maps strings to lists, where each list element is a map of ...", clojure.spec makes it more formal and verifiable. This is very useful when working with data, and is another example of where Clojure's pragmatism shines; the language is dynamic in its core, but when you need static checking - it's there, optionally (core.typed is another option for a more statically typed flavor).

The right approach to object-orientation

Historically, Lisp programmers weren't the biggest proponents of OOP. This doesn't mean that OOP has absolutely no value in Lisp-y languages, however. Common Lisp has had CLOS for decades, and Clojure also comes with an array of OO-like features.

That said, Clojure's flavor of OOP is particularly powerful and tends to discourage bad practices. Clojure uses "protocols", which are a kind of interfaces, and encourages thinking in terms of protocols rather than in terms of classes with inheritance hierarchies, sort of like Go. Add to that an ability to do true multiple dispatch and you have a powerful modeling tool at your fingertips.

Built-in support for concurrency and parallelism

It wouldn't be a real language of the 2000s without powerful support for concurrency and parallelism right at the core. Clojure supports this in many ways, which are interleaved.

First, it's a functional language with persistent data structures. Persistent data structures are effectively immutable, which makes them very attractive in a multi-threaded context. Clojure has a great implementation of persistent data structures even for things like vectors (which are quite challenging to implement in an efficient manner). This is a bigger deal than may originally appear. Pure functions are often great in theory but fail in practice due to too much copying of non-trivial data structures; Clojure's elegant usage of persistent data structures solves this problem, making pure functions efficient and thus much more applicable to a wide array of problems.

Second, Clojure doesn't lock itself in the closet of purism and does support lower-level primitives for concurrency and mutation, where needed. Atoms are built-in mutable state units with atomic updates. Refs and transactions go further, implementing STM.

Third, Clojure comes with a bunch of concurrency tools built in. Promises, futures and threads leverage the underlying JVM's threading utilities.

Finally, Clojure has a pretty good implementation of Go's CSP in the core.async module. It provides two useful things:

  1. Channels and Go select-like functionality (alts!!) which makes it easy to work with safe concurrent queues and "share data by communicating".
  2. go-blocks with non-blocking primitives that make it possible to write cooperative "green threads" with ease.

Conclusion - try it

Finally, it's important to mention that Clojure is far from being an academic exercise. It's used in production by several companies, and has strong roots in the massive Java ecosystem. Clojure's interoperability with Java is seamless - Java code can be called from Clojure with no special provisions, and all core Clojure entities are Java objects deep under the hood.

On the client side, Clojurescript has been gaining traction recently as another language-compiled-to-JS option. It brings the elegance of Clojure to client-side programming, among with some unique features like core.async for callback-free concurrency.

This doesn't mean that you should only consider Clojure as a fit for your next project. On the contrary, I recommend learning if even if there's little chance of using it in production any time soon. In fact, this was exactly my situation, Clojure is a great language to expand your programming horizons; who knows, maybe in the future you'll find it useful for some real work. If you do, great! If you don't, learning it will positively affect how you use other programming languages.

item.title: Re: Riemann (213 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://borretti.me/article/re-riemann, See on Hacker News

A fun thing about living in Australia is that most things happen overnight, so reading the news in the morning is like a gacha game. You pick up the phone and scroll through notifications of world-historic events: elections won, wars begun, models released, conjectures proven or refuted. Today’s pull was a Discord notification saying: “they proved riemann :/”.

This part of the announcement caught my attention (bold mine):

I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis. In fact, the method easily extends much further, resolving the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and I expect, with more time, the Extended Riemann Hypothesis too. Claude and I have also formalized the arguments without assumptions. It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater.

It was my secret in my student days that my plans were for this problem in decades, which meant then that I tried to become familiar with all tools that I could possibly recognize in the problem when it was time. Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line. No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line. I had us on the line of combining two quite different ideas present in a toy setting, one of which was already new and shocking, making very simple one of the shadows of Riemann over which we mathematicians felt most triumph. I guided us to the right situation analogous to that toy setting, and then Claude began to leave me in awe.

Compare the above to Ayn Rand’s account of watching the launch of Apollo 11:

How do you descend from a state of pure exaltation?

What we had seen, in naked essentials—but in reality, not in a work of art—was the concretized abstraction of man’s greatness.

The meaning of the sight lay in the fact that when those dark red wings of fire flared open, one knew that one was not looking at a normal occurrence, but at a cataclysm which, if unleashed by nature, would have wiped man out of existence—and one knew also that this cataclysm was planned, unleashed, and controlled by man, that this unimaginable power was ruled by his power and, obediently serving his purpose, was making way for a slender, rising craft. One knew that this spectacle was not the product of inanimate nature, like some aurora borealis, or of chance, or of luck, that it was unmistakably human—with “human,” for once, meaning grandeur—that a purpose and a long, sustained, disciplined effort had gone to achieve this series of moments, and that man was succeeding, succeeding, succeeding! For once, if only for seven minutes, the worst among those who saw it had to feel—not “How small is man by the side of the Grand Canyon!”—but “How great is man and how safe is nature when he conquers it!”

Rand’s essay says: how great is Man! How noble in reason, how infinite in faculty! The Riemann announcement reads like a suicide note, or like the farewell message of a terminally-ill person who’s about to undergo euthanasia: “I shall live on in my child, Claude. It is natural to feel this is an end, but as the Buddha taught us, there is no self. Does a wave die when it breaks?” and so on.

There’s a mural by Diego Rivera I love. It’s called Man, Controller of the Universe:

It’s a collage of images of science, technology, history, cells, galaxies, the universe at the nanoscale and the exascale. And at the center there is a man, his hands grasping the controls. He wears a complicated expression: the weight of responsibility for the future, the weight of autonomy.

And I see this mural, and think: how great is Man! Our life is like a breath of air, we were beset by illness and hunger and cold, millions and hundreds of millions died in plagues. And yet we—sick, hungry, short-lived—learned the system of the world, crawled out of the caves, brought nature to heel, walked on the Moon. The last shall be first! And eyes that are clouded with age have seen the furthest stars, and the lives of a cell, and the worlds of Cantor and Hilbert: the invisible world that waited forever. We are dust and ashes, and yet our minds bestride the universe. How great is Man!

And when I read the Riemann announcement, when I read Machines of Loving Grace: humanity is not at the center. Claude is at the center. We are hidden in the margins, passive recipients of manna from Claude. How great is Claude! How noble in reason, how infinite in benevolence! The dancing star, the living word!

It’s a betrayal and a surrender. Man is a bridge, a rusty old bridge that we can neither preserve nor restore. We can move forward and become as the gods, or retreat back into the caves. And the dream of the AI companies, and of most people in AI safety and effective altruism and rationalism; is instead that we should lie down in a warm bath, watch the demons we summoned dance in the sky, and slip away. Why live? Our servants can do that for us. Why should we explore, discover, invent, succeed, become more, struggle, win, become divine? We don’t want to be more. We don’t want anything.
